en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Seven Stories,
Chapter on Gandhāra.
6. The Susīma Jātaka “Black were the hairs that formerly grew upon the head in their proper places;”
"Having seen those white [hairs] today, O Susīma, practice the Dhamma;
it is time for the holy life.
"O King, this grey hair is mine alone, not yours."
"My very head, my supreme limb—
I spoke falsely, saying 'I shall bring about your welfare.
O best of kings, forgive this one offense."
"You are young and handsome, O King,
like a young bamboo shoot just sprouted;
rule your kingdom and look upon me."
"Do not pursue what is transient, O Lord of Men.
"I see this young maiden,
with eyes like a deer, slender-limbed and well-proportioned;"
Like a black flame flickering and spreading,
she moves along as if enticing men;
I see that woman later as darkness.
Whether eighty or ninety years of age,
he walks leaning on a staff, trembling,
moving like a rafter that has become bent.
Thus, reflecting upon that very same thing,
I lay alone in the midst of my bed,
observing: "I too am thus."
One should not delight in the household life; it is time for the holy life.
This attachment to the household that comes from living at home is like hanging by a rope.
"Thus having cut [the bonds], the wise go forth,
indifferent, having abandoned sensual pleasure.
Thus ends the sixth Jātaka, the Susīma-jātaka.
